allies.rationale_text: Systems-thinking helps supply-and-demand see how customers, suppliers, and competitors interact instead of treating price in isolation.
allies.affinity_rationale: Canonical describes supply and demand as a core component of understanding economic system dynamics
allies.activation_condition: When market analysis requires understanding how supply-side and demand-side elements interact systemically

allies.rationale_text: Risk-assessment helps supply-and-demand translate market pressure changes into decision-relevant exposure rather than vague intuition.
allies.source_quote: objective starting point for making decisions
allies.affinity_rationale: Risk assessment supports supply-demand analysis by quantifying potential disruptions to market equilibrium
allies.activation_condition: When evaluating risks to supply chains or demand patterns requires structured assessment

antagonists.rationale_text: System-1 undermines supply-and-demand by driving emotional, impulsive decisions that override the rational cost-benefit analysis the model assumes actors will perform.
antagonists.source_quote: The model assumes that economic behavior is primarily analytical and rational. However, much of human decision-making is influenced by the emotional, fast, associative System 1 thinking (known as the reflexive brain) rather than the slow, deliberative System 2 (reflective brain).
antagonists.affinity_rationale: Canonical describes bounded rationality and the planner-doer conflict where impulsive System 1 deviates from rational economic predictions
antagonists.activation_condition: When impulsive decision-making deviates from rational cost-benefit analysis predicted by economic models

structured_tensions.tension_text: Supply-and-demand conflicts with status-quo-bias when pricing and capacity remain fixed despite shifted market equilibrium.
Supply-and-demand conflicts with anchoring when an initial price expectation distorts objective assessment of market conditions.
